PRESENTATIONS
1.  Potential Ballot Measure - Utility Users Tax
  Recommendation:
  No action required by the Commission. This is a presentation only.

  Finance Director/City Treasurer Hui presented the staff report.

  The Commission discussed building department inspections and in particular, concerns
  about consistency over fire inspection service deliveries from a budget standpoint,
  considering one previous inspector handled the entire City, and now, each of the three
  inspectors handle three different areas of Vernon. Staff confirmed there was previously
  one Vernon Fire Inspector who provided fire inspections to the entire city, and the
  current model of Los Angeles County Fire Department, provides for three LA County
  Fire Department Fire Inspectors who are responsible for conducting fire inspections on
  building developments. Staff informed the Commission that there are efforts being
  made through ongoing meetings to discuss concerns brought forth by both the City and
  by LA County Fire Chiefs over service deliveries and inspection-related responsibilities.

  The Commission discussed the sunset of the current 6% utility users tax, the evolution
  of the utility user’s taxation over time, and expressed concerns over it potentially
  evolving into a permanent funding source. The Commission expressed their preference
  to have staff present flexible options to the 6% rate and explore proposing a sunset
  date. Staff confirmed the sunset of the current tax is 2028, and relayed concerns on
  global impacts surrounding the utility user tax as it relates to the whole organization,
  and affirmed staff have contingency plans in place in the event the measure does not
  pass. The Commission expressed a desire to have staff to include and engage
  businesses in conversations through a series of informational meetings over an
  extended period of time and to provide in-depth analyses with comparative data to
  surrounding cities.

  In response to questions from the Commission, staff provided information on electric
  revenue shortfalls, impacts to local businesses who must weigh the costs to conduct
  business in California, and the recent efforts to leverage state and federal legislative
  support through a memorandum of understanding with five neighboring cities, newly
  known as “The Big Five” with the goal to garner support to fund capital infrastructure
  projects for smaller cities in the LA area, like Vernon.

  The Commission expressed their desire to be provided with the opportunity to give
  feedback and make recommendations to the City Council through the commission
  discussion and recommendation process. Staff assured the Commission that their

Subject
Proposed Fiscal Year (FY) 2026-2027 General Fee Schedule

Recommendation
Receive and file the proposed FY 2026-27 General Fee Schedule and request that staff present
the proposed General Fee Schedule to Council for review and adoption at a public hearing on
April 7, 2026.

Background
The City provides services to individuals or businesses for a fee. When fees do not fully recover
the cost of providing a service, it results in a subsidy that may affect the City’s ability to fund
programs and services relied upon by the community. Examples of City services for which fees
are charged include the issuance of building, development and health and environmental control
permits.

As part of the annual budget process, the City’s General Fee Schedule is reviewed to ensure
that the fees are established in accordance with applicable federal and State laws and accurately
reflect the scope and cost of services provided. A draft fee schedule is prepared and presented
to the Business and Industry Commission (BIC) and the City Council for review and consideration
(Attachment 1).

In March 2025, the City engaged Willdan Finance Services (Willdan) to conduct a User Fee
Study. The study calculated the full cost of service and developed fee schedules for activities in
the Building, Engineering, Health and Environmental Control, Police and administrative service
areas. Fees related to Fire Prevention Services were not reviewed, as those services are
provided by and approved through the Los Angeles County Fire Department.

The proposed General Fee Schedule includes revisions to Engineering and Health and
Environmental Control permit fees to better align with the cost of service. Engineering fee
updates include revisions to grading fees and fees related to type of work performed and the
addition of transportation permit fees, including overload hauling permits established by the
California Department of Transportation (Caltrans). Health and Environmental Control permit fee
changes include revisions to food plan check and CUPA plan check fees, as well as the addition
of local agency oversight services fees, such as environmental site assessment review fee and
a miscellaneous fee. A redline of the proposed changes is attached to this report for reference
(Attachment 2).

To ensure that the public has access to the most updated Fire Prevention Service fees, which
are administered and controlled by the Los Angeles County Fire Department, the proposed Fee
Schedule includes a link to the Los Angeles County Fire Prevention Fee website rather than a
detailed listing of fees.

Fees structures may vary among cities due to differences in community needs, organizational
structures, and service delivery responsibilities. As a result, direct fee comparisons across

 jurisdictions can be challenging. Where feasible, the City’s proposed fees were compared with
those of similar cities to confirm that the fees are reasonable and consistent with the level and
type of service provided.

Ongoing annual reviews and adjustments to the fee schedule, particularly to reflect increases in
labor-related costs, will help ensure the City is appropriately reimbursed for the cost of services
provided. The proposed Fiscal Year 2026-27 General Fee Schedule will be presented to the City
Council for consideration and adoption at a public hearing in April 2026.

Fiscal Impact
There is no fiscal impact associated with this report.

Subject
Update on Los Angeles County Proposed Half-Cent Sales Tax Ballot Measure

Recommendation
A. Receive and file the report on the Los Angeles County proposed half-cent sales tax measure
to be placed on the June 2, 2026 Statewide Direct Primary Election ballot; and
B. Provide feedback regarding a potential quarter-cent local sales tax measure to be considered
by City Council at their Regular Meeting on March 3, 2026.

Background
On February 10, 2026, the Los Angeles County Board of Supervisors adopted a resolution
ordering and calling a special election for a countywide general retail transactions and use (sales)
tax measure to be placed on the June 2, 2026 Statewide Direct Primary Election ballot. The
measure will ask voters whether to increase the County sales tax rate by one half cent (½-cent)
to offset federal funding cuts to public health services. If approved by voters, it is anticipated that
the tax would generate approximately $1 billion annually over a five-year period. As drafted, the
June ballot measure would seek a legislative exemption from the existing two percent (2%)
statutory cap on county/local sales taxes and preserve one quarter percent (¼ %) in sales tax
capacity under the statutory cap.

The proposed spending plan allocates approximately forty seven percent (47%) for no cost or
reduced cost health care services, five percent (5%) for school based health programs, ten
percent (10%) for public health initiatives, five percent (5%) for Medicaid outreach and enrollment
efforts, two and a half percent (2.5%) for correctional health services, twenty two percent (22%)
for financial support to the Department of Health Services, five percent (5%) for non-profit
hospitals, two and a half percent (2.5%) for in home supportive services, and one percent (1%)
for public health programs in Pasadena and Long Beach. Our department was not included with
those public health jurisdictions because we do not offer the same range of resident services as
Pasadena and Long Beach.

Current Sales Tax
In Vernon, the cumulative sales tax rate is currently 10.50 %, which consists of the statewide
sales tax rate of 7.25 % and county/local taxes totaling 3.25 %. Although California Revenue and
Taxation Code Section 7251.1 sets the maximum county/local transactions and use tax—or
statutory cap—at two percent (2%), several countywide sales tax measures have been
authorized through special legislation exempting them from that cap.

Among these exempt measures are L.A. County Measure R (½ cent), Measure M (½ cent), and
Measure A (½ cent). With these exemptions, one quarter percent (¼ %) remains available under
the two percent (2%) county/local statutory sales tax cap.

Voter approval of recent countywide sales tax measures like Measure H and Measure A has
prompted discussion among local agencies regarding the effectiveness of these measures and
the fairness of local returns compared to total tax resources generated within individual

  Item 3  Page 40 of 42
 jurisdictions. For example, Measure H (approved in 2017 by approximately 69% of countywide
voters) levied a one quarter percent (¼ %) transactions and use tax for ten years to address
homelessness. In Vernon, it is estimated that this measure generated over $10 million prior to its
repeal in 2024. Of these resources, only a few thousand dollars have been returned to our
community to help address homelessness.

More recently, Measure A (approved in 2024 by approximately 58% of countywide voters)
repealed Measure H and levied a one half percent (½ %) transactions and use tax to remain in
effect until repealed by voters. In Vernon, it is estimated that roughly $3 million is generated
annually. According to the Measure A Allocation Methodology, at least fifteen percent (15%) is
allocated to cities, councils of governments, and/or the County (for unincorporated areas) for
homelessness prevention programs and affordable housing initiatives.

Discussion
Without special legislation to exempt the June Measure from the two percent (2%) county and
local statutory sales tax cap, passage of the measure would cause the combined rate to exceed
the cap. In that case, the measure could not be fully implemented—and might not be
implemented at all—or would only take effect up to the remaining capacity. This, in turn, could
prevent the City from later enacting its own local sales tax measure.

Adding to the uncertainty, if both the June Measure and a local city sales tax measure appear on
the June ballot and both are approved by voters—but the June Measure does not obtain special
legislative authority to exceed the cap—the City’s ability to implement its own measure in Vernon
would remain unclear. The outcome could depend on which measure receives the greater
number of votes within the City or which measure the California Department of Tax and Fee
Administration (CDTFA) determines to implement, following guidance from the California
Attorney General.

Given this uncertainty, it may be prudent for the City to preserve local control over tax revenues
by pursuing its own one quarter cent (¼ %) sales tax measure, rather than relying on future
countywide programs that may provide only limited local return or benefit.

Next Steps
On February 17, 2026, the City Council received an update from staff regarding the County’s
proposed general retail transactions and use (sales) tax measure on the June 2, 2026 Statewide
Direct Primary Election ballot as well as information regarding the City’s current sales tax and
potential impact to the City’s ability to capture the one quarter percent (¼ %) of sales tax that
currently remains available. At the meeting, the City Council tabled the discussion on the
possibility of a local sales tax measure to the Regular Meeting on March 3, 2026 and directed
staff to prepare all necessary documentation to consider proceeding with placing a local
transaction and use tax measure before voters at the June 2, 2026 election. To qualify for the
June 2, 2026 ballot, the Council must take all required actions no later than Friday, March 6, 2026,
and must also adopt a unanimous resolution declaring a fiscal emergency in order to place the
measure on that ballot. Staff noted there are potential legal and policy implications associated
with declaring a fiscal emergency, and the long-term impacts of such a declaration remain
uncertain.

Information is being presented to the Business and Industry Commission at a Special Meeting
on February 19, 2026 for feedback regarding the consideration of a potential quarter-cent local
sales tax measure. The Commission’s feedback will be shared with the City Council at their
Regular Meeting on March 3, 2026.

  The Commission discussed their concerns over the cost of living in California compared
  to the rest of the United States, raising taxes in general, especially in light of the public
  being very aware of publicized tax-payer fraud in the state of Minnesota, and recently
  raised concerns over tax-payer fraud in California, the general lack of accountability in
  government, the unknown impacts of raising sales tax to local businesses, and how
  scenarios related to the LA County sales tax measure might play out. Additionally, the
  Commission expressed concerns over the ramifications of declaring a fiscal emergency
  in order to hold a special election, such as the optics for the City and businesses.

  City Administrator Saeki explained the necessity of declaring a fiscal emergency in
  order to hold a special election. He clarified that if the LA County measure failed, and
  the Vernon measure succeeds, the sales tax rate in Vernon would go from 10.25% to
  10.75%, and added the value of the ¼ percent sales tax would be approximately $1.5
  to $1.6 million annually and that portion of the tax would stay locally. He reiterated that
  a fiscal emergency must be declared to hold a special election to put a measure on the
  ballot. He explained a messaging and communications plan to maintain local control of
  local tax dollars to support Vernon and not outside entities such as Los Angeles County,
  which would receive the largest portion of tax dollars, with Vernon receiving little to no
  allocation.

  He assured the Commission that the City’s messaging plan would include information
  about the trustworthiness, good governance, and reputation of the City’s stewardship
  of the City’s coffers. He explained that the set of circumstances causes uncertainty and
  there hasn’t been precedence set, and staff is researching the possible outcomes and
  strategy.

  Commissioner Ybarra expressed support to try and secure the 1/4 percent sales tax in
  order to keep local control of tax dollars.
  The Commission expressed concerns about rising costs for businesses, inflation,
  insurance, operating costs, and competing with other businesses in neighboring cities
  with lower sales tax rates.
  City Administrator Saeki shared a brief history on Measure H and Measure A, which,
  based on historical perspective, the electorate will likely pass the upcoming LA County
  tax measure. He opined the LA County tax measure’s 5-year sunset would likely be
  extended in the future.
  The Commission also discussed their concerns to keep local tax dollars in Vernon,
  options to sunset or extend the potential ¼ cent sales tax, and the sunsetting Utility
  User’s Tax and Special Safety Parcel Tax, the messaging plan for placing the sales tax
  on the ballot, and questioned whether Vernon would extend or let the tax sunset.
  City Administrator Saeki explained that the City acts at the direction of the Council and
  the Business and Industry Commission, and informed that the Council directed staff to
  undertake a thorough cost-of-business study in Vernon to reveal the parity of doing
  business in the City that would include different scenarios regarding the UUT.

  The Commission wished to explore the cost of holding a special election with placing
  the ¼ sales tax on the next General Municipal Election in 2027. The Commission
  expressed their favor in keeping sales tax monies in Vernon’s control to benefit Vernon
  rather than giving control and the benefit to LA County’s coffers.

  City Administrator Saeki informed that the number of registered voters in the City is 111
  and added the City would take a neutral position on any potential ballot measures.

  The Commission expressed its desire to support the ballot measure and, in return,
  would like to see incentives for businesses such as changes to the business license
  fees and have these incentives codified. The Commission was interested in the sales
  tax breakdown across different types of businesses, including wholesale and retail.

  Marisa Olguin of the Vernon Chamber of Commerce provided comments supporting
  keeping the potential ¼ sales tax in Vernon to create equity within the business
  community and indicated it would be positive for the General fund as the City seeks
  balance of supporting businesses while experiencing challenges to the General Fund.
  She expressed there being a risk of going to an 11 percent sales tax as businesses are
  competing for cities with lower sales tax. She indicated the Chamber has supported the
  City historically to add to the General Fund; however, she indicated she would not take
  a Chamber position until more data is provided, more questions are answered, and
  options are further discussed.

  City Administrator Saeki informed that the cost of holding a special election could be
  averted by placing a ballot measure on the next general municipal election to seek the
  ¼ percent tax, if the tax is still available. He reiterated that this situation has not been
  tested so any outcomes would be speculated.
